findings.observation: Winds adds another meaning of a familiar-looking word. Goes is simpler; the current line is understandable with the illustration.
“The Moon shows again” is an unnatural use of shows for an emerging object.

The Moon is small against the sky in the sequence. The page is coherent, but a larger teaching focal point may help a child locate it. This is a readability suggestion, not a confirmed rendering failure.
Native page 2 uses hundreds of shaded hairlike feather strokes and textured straw. This breaks the whole-image flat cartoon standard and differs from the simpler chick on later pages.
A soft bite is understandable in context, but something soft sounds more natural.
The opening sounds like words were removed to fit the page limit; it does not name a destination.
Line, joins and says are avoidable secondary meanings in a beginner safety sequence. The pictures already supply the intended objects and signal meaning.
The transformation should name the wheel so a beginner can connect the folded paper to the visible object. Preserve the established fantasy rule.
“Shelters its soft abdomen” explains a useful animal name with harder words.
“Different shapes share a group” uses abstract classification language and makes shapes the actors. The picture points to the smooth spoon beside the smooth pebble.
“A Little First” is an elliptical title with no named object. “The crackers wait” adds unnecessary personification instead of explaining the visible storage for later.

At native size the yellow button is visible as two narrow crescents around a dark slit; its flat face and the pressing hand are not clear. This makes the failed flat-push action weaker than the explicit side-on button shown on p3. The soft folded flap on p4–5 is physically possible, so no definite fastening/anatomy failure is asserted.

“Zoe taps an answer” makes answer mean a musical response. The preparation acknowledges this figurative sense, but it adds an avoidable second meaning for beginning ESL readers when the intended event is simply another drum turn.
“From hill to river to sea. One connected path.” ends in a compressed abstract label. A child can follow the same water in an ordinary complete sentence.
“Slips around” is understandable but flows is more literal. The visual instruction route and fresh-water sense can be supported more directly.

The sequence is coherent, and pupa is intentionally oral vocabulary. Naming it on p5 would clarify “inside.” Current larva/pupa definitions explain one technical stage using another technical stage; book-specific visible descriptions would be easier to say to ESL children.

Native images show six touching road blocks and two loose blocks. There is no clearly bounded one-block gap before a final turn. The source requires seven blocks placed, one loose block and one gap after Zoe adds her block. The p6 visual question expects evidence absent from its illustration.

“My cheese has no cracker now” gives the cheese an unnatural possession-like sentence. “This bite has a cracker” is an awkward abstract description of an ordinary snack. Neither sounds like natural child speech or narration.
In the postal journey, “has come a long way” can describe literal distance. A more direct ending is useful ESL polish, but the phrase is not a firm confusing-idiom failure in this context.
The opening has not named Zoe, yet p2 says “Her cup”; “clips both” also requires carrying two unnamed objects from fragments on p1. Name the owner and the two things being clipped.
“Which three objects now have different or unchanged colors?” combines two opposed abstract conditions and asks which three when the intended response is to name each visible color.

The sequence repeatedly reserves much of the image for empty room and floor. The clips are clear at native size but small in the 396px review tiles. Consider tighter framing around the three objects and the clipping hands; actual reader-size usability was not exercised, so this is a composition recommendation, not a measured app failure.

“The sea falls” does not specify its water level. “Rock holds the water around the sides” and “the rock dip keeps a pool” compress the mechanism into unnatural language. The visible falling water and trapped pool can be explained with ordinary complete sentences.

The picture shows supports changing angle at joints. “Move at their joints” is more precise than “bend at their joints” without implying that the rigid bars bend. This is an editorial precision suggestion, not an externally verified engineering fault.
“Still legs” can briefly be read as remaining legs rather than legs that do not move. The picture and preceding pages resolve the meaning; an explicit action would be easier for some ESL readers.

“After the last shed” uses an unfamiliar noun sense of shed, although preparation teaches shed as a verb. “Grows wings in stages” adds an abstract summary to an already visible sequence. Use the taught verb and the visible final wings.
“Do the job of the final wings” hides the intended visible comparison behind a job metaphor. Ask about the wing pads directly, then compare with the long wings on p6.

The terms are useful science vocabulary, not outdated words. Replace “the adult’s basic shape” and “small parts” with the visible grasshopper/wing relationship if these definitions are spoken to children.
Both pages call the surface a wall. The actual art, props, image briefs and visual discussion use a freestanding white screen. This teaches the wrong concrete object word.
“Split the two light-passing sheets into separate groups” uses an invented compound and a long teacher-style question. Name the familiar materials.

The repeated “one” on p7 can be replaced with the material names. The red car is enlarged for the panel comparison and looks longer on p8 than its small earlier form. The brief intentionally requests one long car; the native images do not clearly prove a duplicate car, so this is a continuity polish item, not an asserted AI anatomy failure.

“The cup stays empty” is logically possible after the repair, but it adds an unnecessary negative observation after the helpful watering action. The current illustration shows the completed action, so retain it or show the pour if changing to ongoing action.
Page 8 says the paper dog “takes a bow”. Knowing the stage idiom is unnecessary to follow the shared puppet play; the picture does not explain its meaning independently.
“Drops short” (p2) and “goes wide” (p7) require sports idioms where direct descriptions would teach the pictured positions.
“The gentle ramp gives it a rolling route” is an abstract, alliterative summary instead of the visible action the child has just solved.
“Bank” is a useful concrete geography word in this story, not outdated language. A brief oral gloss can prevent the money-bank interpretation.
The pond is visible in earlier illustrations. A plain arrival statement is easier and avoids implying that it has only just become visible.
The current gloss “represents or shows something else” supplies another abstract synonym. The concept is relevant; the oral explanation can be simpler.
Page 8 introduces “shelters”, “structures”, and figurative “jobs” together. The scientific distinction can be stated through visible water and sleeping-place actions.
“Nymph” and “adult” are necessary teaching vocabulary, supported by the pictures. “A young insect stage” makes the oral gloss unnecessarily abstract.
The apple core does not reappear. “Comes Back” is a metaphor for its contribution to compost and a new plant.
The current definition “things living things need to grow” repeats “things” and is less useful than a plant-specific oral explanation.
Page 2 says “goes inside”. Its native image already places Kit and Zoe in the kitchen beside the indoor shelf; page 1 also starts there. The intended action is walking to the shelf.
“Picture the card” uses picture as a mental verb; “I keep losing one bit” treats a forgotten item as a lost physical piece. Both obscure the otherwise concrete memory task.
The unused entry “remind” is glossed as “help someone bring a thought back”, another metaphor. Use the actual story verb “remember” instead.
“What is present, and what is still missing?” is more abstract than the visible locations of these specific picnic items.
“His hand closes around the red ribbon” obscures the simple action of picking it up and gives the body part the grammatical action.
“Pulls the bow” is imprecise because pulling different parts can tighten or undo it. The image shows the finished two loops.
The final sentence makes the list “Growing, carrying, and setting out” its subject. The sequence is correct, but named actors and direct verbs are easier to follow.

Native pp2 and5 merge arrowheads four and five into one X on the continuous line. Page 5 is the visual-assessment page, whose expected answer specifically identifies the fifth arrow pointing left. The cover and pp3/4 show the two opposed heads separately, so this is also inconsistent across the sequence.

The sequence unnecessarily uses “follow the points”, “one point sends his finger”, “paper now gives one clear route”, “repaired place”, and “a red tip waits”. These expressions are harder than the actual pointing, drawing and marking actions.

“A dark top does not mean a cool inside” and “heat escapes” are understandable with teaching, but the same scientific point can use direct sentences. The topic words lava, crust and solid should remain.
The opening uses “solid body” and “small frozen body”. Children may read body as an animal body; naming ice and dust is clearer and retains the comet concept.
The current “an icy body” gloss repeats the same secondary meaning instead of explaining it.

“The stone stays outside the otter’s body” is a technically framed qualification that does not help a child understand this action. The defining evidence is that the otter uses the stone to reach food.
“What made the stone a tool in this sequence?” contains unnecessary editorial vocabulary (“sequence”) and abstract classification phrasing.

“Has mated” introduces an unexplained verb beyond this shell-growth explanation. “One body and its shell grow together” is an unnatural summary. This is a language-load issue, not an objection to teaching reproduction.
The oral prompt asks how this shell differs from an empty shell “an animal might move into”. That extra hypothetical animal is not needed to assess the printed shell-growth concept.
“Clutch” and “mature” do not occur in the page text. “Fully grown and able to reproduce” adds another advanced verb. This distracts from the shell lesson.
“The water test puts them in different groups” gives an abstract test agency. The observed salt-versus-sand result is clearer as the subject.
“A solid piece with an ordered form” uses two abstract words to explain a new noun. Salt-specific language connects the gloss to the picture.

Native pp2 and4 have dense mottled/brushy bark and soil, speckled highlights, hyper-textured surfaces and camera-like focus blur. They differ sharply from the simple outlined cartoon scenes on pp1/3/5–8. The current style standard explicitly rejects hyper-textured material rendering and painted backgrounds even when the animal outlines are clean.

“The busy patch”, “its cover”, “discarded wrapper”, and “shade and damp shelter remain” are vague, formal or abstract. These phrases add no science meaning that the pictured home and litter action cannot express directly.
The page text says “dead plant pieces” and “soft wood”; “decay” is not printed. It could be an extension word, but should not displace oral support for a word actually needed by the reader.
The abstract ending makes spoken ideas into objects that fit inside a box. The child must unpack a metaphor instead of seeing what Kit packed.
“Your loud bit” is unnatural, vague dialogue. It conceals the concrete link between the falling blocks, the stray line and the new branch.
The fully expanded question sounds stiff in child dialogue; a contraction is more natural.
The current question is answerable but “misunderstand” adds language demand.
The cup is tilted under running water without a visible holding hand or stable support. Its body appears separated from the sink by a shadow; the tipping action is not physically explained.
“The river does not belong to the sink” introduces an irrelevant ownership idea. State why cleaning the water matters to the animals and plants.
The same book uses “plant” for a water-cleaning facility and living things. The facility meaning is not explained in languagePrep.
“Pocket” consistently names a detached blue zip pouch. For ESL children, the named everyday object and its picture should agree. The fantasy rule is clear; the object name is the problem.
The island-size sentence is less direct than necessary, though it is accurate and supported.
The grammatical subject of “struck” is the smaller crater. A crater is the resulting mark, not the impacting rock. This reverses the cause being taught.
“More than spots” and “hold clues” produce a vague summary ending. Name the rocks, the craters and what their overlapping shapes tell us.
The definition replaces “impact” with the equally difficult “collision.” Oral support should explain the new word using familiar actions.

Pollination is an unexplained causal step. It is absent from languagePrep, and the page image shows a wilted flower and growing pod without the pollen event. Keep the science term but provide direct support.
“A new root begins the journey again” is an unnecessary abstract metaphor at the exact point where a literal life-cycle ending would help.
“Matter to the next plant” asks children to decode an abstract relationship before answering the science question.
“Into the clip tray it goes” uses literary inversion, and “these groups tell” is abstract. Keep the sorting result visible and concrete.
“Poor rule for this sorting task” is adult assessment wording, not a natural question to an ESL child.
The colon list followed by “the battery connects two parts of the day” turns an energy-storage explanation into an abstract slogan.
“Electrical circuit” uses a form of the target word and introduces another technical term. The definition is less accessible than the word it explains.
“Materials and care” is vague and introduces an undeveloped environmental point. A concrete material example would help if this page is retained.
A puddle being “the wrong part of the day” is an awkward abstract way to express that the picture no longer matches Zoe’s memory.

The large wall and floor fills have faint cloudy/mottled texture rather than clean flat fills or a few smooth cel-shaded shapes. This is a finish mismatch with the current whole-image style standard, not a malformed-character finding.
“Belong in the same picture” is understandable after the sequence but still more abstract than the depicted memory.

The large wall and floor fills have faint cloudy/mottled texture rather than clean flat fills or a few smooth cel-shaded shapes. This is a finish mismatch with the current whole-image style standard, not a malformed-character finding.
“They do not move the traffic themselves” is an odd literal negation that blurs the practical safety message. Say directly that people still check traffic.
“More than one way to say the same thing” is a vague recap. Name the different signals.
“A giant bow carries the shadow fan” makes the action a strange agent. Name Kit bending and the shadow copying him.

The large wall and floor fills have faint cloudy/mottled texture rather than clean flat fills or a few smooth cel-shaded shapes. This is a finish mismatch with the current whole-image style standard, not a malformed-character finding.
A flat hand is not the clearest reason the shadow cannot pick up the fan. The story can state that it is only a shadow.
The rock walking and dune jumping are unprompted personifications introduced only to negate them. Use the fixed rock and moving sand as the evidence.
The question repeats the unnecessary image of a hill jumping. Ask about the mechanism directly.
“A hill can travel” is a supported metaphor, but literal movement is easier for this audience.
“Took a bite” and Earth “stood in the way” add nonliteral language to a science conclusion. The book has enough literal evidence for a direct explanation.
Saying the wing did not turn into a flower introduces an unnecessary impossible event. Explain the actual visible background.
The retrospective “what seemed missing was there all along” is unnecessarily indirect, although the sequence supports it.
“The soft stage does not last for the rest of the crab’s life” is a cumbersome negative that restates the first sentence.
“The empty shape cannot follow” personifies the shell. The following double-crab negation is less clear than naming the crab and empty shell.
“Fruits need not look alike” is formal phrasing for a straightforward comparison.
“Catch the same bright spill” uses a metaphor and a technical noun without explaining either. State where less light reaches.
“The path, hedge, and window share the night” is a vague poetic ending. The final image actually has a lit upstairs room and dark porch/path; use that concrete contrast.
“Finds the words” and the double meaning of “holds up” add idiomatic interpretation to a concrete puppet story. End with Kit visibly performing.
“Keep both the laugh and the rest” treats abstract effects as objects; “one last laugh” also hides Kit’s request for a funny ending.
The garden cannot literally hold a storm; it holds rainwater. “Journey of the rain: pause, spread, soak” is compressed and abstract beside the otherwise concrete runoff sequence.
Current explanation is coherent and supported, but “cannot keep carrying the same load” can be made more direct without removing sediment or deposition.
“Earth faces almost all of the sunlit half” is indirect and can suggest Earth itself changes orientation to cause the phase. Say what people on Earth can see.

Seeds “hold the next generation”, a “larger web of living things”, and “one meal connects two lives” demand three unnecessary metaphors. Keep pollination, nectar and seeds, with their pictured mechanism.
“Use another place” does not explain what the new body enables. The definition “a new group of offspring in a life cycle” is harder than the word being taught.
“Life histories”, “surface-breathing routine”, “despite their fishlike outline” and “connected features” sound like an adult report. Keep mammal and the milk/breathing evidence.
“Saved water by keeping it useful” is an abstract evaluation. State the result the illustration actually proves.
“Maybe I should keep it all” can mean keeping both halves rather than keeping the whole picture private. The distinction drives the next action.
“Their plan has room… It works…” describes a planning outcome in adult report language. The illustration shows two children sitting while the caretaker walks past.
“My surprise took a little finding” is an unfamiliar compressed expression that does not sound like a child speaking.
“The missing ice left its work behind” gives ice human work and replaces the visible evidence with a metaphor.
Vastly, fixed and sharing one small place increase language load without helping the model comparison. Depth and constellation are useful topic terms and should stay supported.
Independent native review of pp3–6 found no firm geometry or continuity defect. A matched end view and side view would demonstrate the changed apparent spacing more directly.
“Two fixed menus”, “a sharp look” and “holds both opportunities” make the feeding comparison unnecessarily figurative. The oral question repeats the menu metaphor.
Relay adds an unrelated race concept to a complex generation sequence; “gave way to the next” is an opaque final idiom. Keep the science and explain later butterflies directly.
The narration repeatedly says “answers” and “these two questions” without ever asking the two questions directly. The grid labels are visible, but an ESL reader must infer the questions.

Independent native review confirms fine continuous simulated wood-grain fibres across the tabletop on pp5–7, strongest on p6. The chart and hands are coherent; the defect is material finish, not sorting logic.
Cover, p1 and p10 have lower-contrast linear grain. Simplification could improve consistency with the repaired close-ups, but these are not additional confirmed texture failures.
“One place can hold…” and “Keeping both takes more…” conclude in abstract adult commentary. The visible walking route and remaining seed heads explain the result.
Native pp4/8 contain dense but crisp grass, seed-head and soil shapes. This is optional focal simplification, not a confirmed painterly failure.
Whole-book follow-up after P1 page 6 repair found the final overview reverted to a tiny shallow-bedding hamster tank, contradicting the preceding deep digging-space lesson.

Final complete sequence reread caught additional avoidable metaphor and abstract phrasing: chimes answered, tools suited a pair, tools followed upward. Use literal action and sound language while preserving the four-tool progression.
Repaired images show the hoof and wing stopping short of a key deep inside; the larger animals cannot enter with their whole bodies. Avoid claiming the hoof physically cannot fit at all.
Align durable story metadata with the repaired small entrance and deep key. The log itself is not narrow.
